stem: Which of the following is the correct definition of **prime cost**?

options.content: Direct materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses
options.rationale: Correct: prime cost is the total of the direct costs.

options.content: Direct materials consumed + direct labour + factory overheads
options.rationale: Factory overheads are added after prime cost.

options.content: Total factory cost adjusted for work in progress
options.rationale: That is the production cost of goods completed.

options.content: Cost of sales of the finished goods sold
options.rationale: Cost of sales is calculated in the income statement.

explanation: Prime cost = direct materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses. Overheads and work in progress come afterwards.

stem: In a bakery, which cost is **direct labour**?

options.content: Wages of the bakers who mix and bake the bread
options.rationale: Correct: they make the product.
A supervisor does not make the bread: indirect wages, a factory overhead.
Office wages are an administration expense, not a manufacturing cost.

options.content: Wages of the van driver delivering bread
options.rationale: Delivery wages are a selling and distribution expense.

explanation: Direct labour is the wages of the workers who actually make the product.

stem: A furniture maker pays a royalty of US\$5 to a designer for every cabinet made. How is the royalty classified?

options.rationale: Overheads cannot be traced to individual units; this cost can.
Correct: it can be traced to each unit made and is neither material nor labour.
A royalty is not a material that becomes part of the cabinet.
It is caused by production, so it is a manufacturing cost.

explanation: Royalties paid per unit produced are the usual example of a direct expense.

stem: Which cost would **not** appear anywhere in a manufacturing account?

options.rationale: This is a factory overhead.
This is added to the cost of raw materials.
Correct: a selling expense, charged in the income statement.
This is a factory overhead.

explanation: Selling, distribution and administration costs go to the income statement, never to the manufacturing account.

stem: Raw materials: opening inventory US\$3,800, purchases US\$41,500, carriage inwards US\$4,600, closing inventory US\$4,900. What is the cost of raw materials consumed?

options.rationale: This leaves out the carriage inwards.
This reverses the inventory adjustments.
This adds the closing inventory instead of deducting it.

stem: Total factory cost is US\$72,600. Work in progress was US\$2,900 at the start of the year and US\$3,700 at the end. What is the production cost of goods completed?

options.rationale: This adds closing and deducts opening work in progress: the wrong way round.
Closing work in progress must be deducted, not added.
Work in progress has been ignored.

hints: Opening work in progress was finished this year; closing work in progress is not yet finished.

stem: Rent of US\$14,400 is for a building used three-quarters as a factory and one-quarter as offices. How is the rent treated?

options.rationale: The office share is an administration expense.

options.content: US\$10,800 prime cost; US\$3,600 factory overhead
options.rationale: Rent is never a direct cost, and the office share is not a factory cost.

options.content: US\$3,600 factory overhead; US\$10,800 income statement expense
options.rationale: The fractions have been swapped.

options.content: US\$10,800 factory overhead; US\$3,600 income statement expense
options.rationale: Correct: only the factory share is a manufacturing cost.

hints: Split the rent first, then classify each part.

stem: A trainee includes the factory supervisor's salary in direct labour instead of factory overheads. What is the effect on the manufacturing account?

options.content: Prime cost and production cost of goods completed are both overstated
options.rationale: Overheads fall by the same amount, so the total is unchanged.

options.content: Prime cost is understated; production cost of goods completed is overstated
options.rationale: Adding to direct labour raises prime cost.

options.content: Neither prime cost nor production cost of goods completed changes
options.rationale: Prime cost does change: direct labour is too high.

options.content: Prime cost is overstated; production cost of goods completed is unchanged
options.rationale: Correct: the cost moves between two parts of the same account.

explanation: Direct labour rises and overheads fall by the same amount: prime cost is too high, but total factory cost and the production cost are correct.
hints: Both direct labour and overheads are inside total factory cost.

stem: Closing work in progress is deducted in the manufacturing account because it is carried forward as an asset.
explanation: True. Half-finished goods are not yet completed production; they appear as a current asset in the statement of financial position.

stem: Depreciation of the delivery van is a factory overhead.
explanation: False. The delivery van is used for selling and distribution, so its depreciation is an income statement expense. Only depreciation of factory assets is an overhead.

stem: A shoe factory in Bulawayo has the costs below. Match each cost with its classification.

left.content: Licence fee paid per pair made

explanation: Materials in the shoe and the makers' wages are direct; a per-pair licence fee is a direct expense; the storekeeper and machine repairs support production (overheads); the sales manager is a selling expense.

stem: Complete the order of the subtotals in a manufacturing account.

payload.template: Cost of raw materials consumed + direct labour + direct expenses = {{blank:a}}. Add factory overheads to give total factory cost, then add {{blank:b}} work in progress and deduct {{blank:c}} work in progress to give the production cost of goods completed.

explanation: Direct costs make prime cost; overheads give total factory cost; then + opening − closing work in progress.

stem: Prime cost is US\$58,200 and factory overheads are US\$19,450.
Raw materials consumed US\$33,750, direct labour US\$21,600, direct expenses US\$950. Calculate prime cost.
explanation: 33,750 + 21,600 + 950 = 56,300. Leaving out the direct expenses gives 55,350.
workedSolution: 1. 33,750 + 21,600 + 950 = 56,300. Leaving out the direct expenses gives 55,350.

stem: For the year ended 31 December 2025 a factory had: raw materials at 1 January US\$2,650, purchases of raw materials US\$29,800, carriage inwards on raw materials US\$640, returns of raw materials US\$390, raw materials at 31 December US\$3,120, direct wages US\$18,700, factory overheads US\$11,750, work in progress at 1 January US\$1,880 and at 31 December US\$2,340. Calculate the production cost of goods completed.
explanation:
1. Raw materials consumed: 2,650 + 29,800 + 640 − 390 − 3,120 = 29,580.
2. Prime cost: 29,580 + 18,700 = 48,280.
3. Total factory cost: 48,280 + 11,750 = 60,030.
4. Production cost: 60,030 + 1,880 − 2,340 = 59,570. Swapping the work in progress figures gives 60,490; ignoring them gives 60,030.
workedSolution:
1. 1. Raw materials consumed: 2,650 + 29,800 + 640 − 390 − 3,120 = 29,580.
2. Prime cost: 29,580 + 18,700 = 48,280.
3. Total factory cost: 48,280 + 11,750 = 60,030.
4. Production cost: 60,030 + 1,880 − 2,340 = 59,570. Swapping the work in progress figures gives 60,490; ignoring them gives 60,030.
hints: Work out raw materials consumed first.
Add overheads, then adjust for work in progress.

stem: A brick maker in Masvingo had a production cost of goods completed of US\$84,150 for 1,700 pallets of bricks. Calculate the production cost per pallet.
hints: Divide the production cost by the number of units completed.

stem: Explain the difference between a **direct** cost and an **indirect** cost in a factory. Give one example of each.

points.description: Direct cost can be traced to each unit made / indirect cannot (shared by all production)
Correct example of each, e.g. direct: materials in the product, makers' wages, royalty per unit; indirect: factory rent, supervisor's salary, depreciation of machinery

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: A direct cost can be traced to each unit produced, such as the timber in a table; an indirect cost is a general factory cost that cannot be traced to particular units, such as the factory rent.

explanation: Traceability to the unit is the test.

stem: Tatenda makes metal gates in Harare. Explain **three** reasons why he needs to know the production cost of each gate completed.

points.description: To set a selling price that covers cost and gives a profit
To value closing inventory of finished goods (and work in progress) in the statements
To control costs / compare with earlier periods or quotes / decide whether to buy in rather than make

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: He can set prices that cover his costs, value his unsold gates correctly at the year end, and spot rising costs or decide whether making a part himself is cheaper than buying it.

explanation: Pricing, inventory valuation and cost control are the main uses.
hints: Think about pricing, valuation and control.
